summary: Discovery call with HelixAI exploring migration from OpenAI hosted usage to Redwood Dedicated or Private. Key themes: compatibility with current OpenAI calls, eval parity (outputs/quality), throughput/latency/cost tradeoffs, private deployment (VPC/KMS), and POC/benchmarking plan.

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-02-25
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Devon (Redwood SE), Ravi (HelixAI Head ML), Ana (Infra), Marcus (CTO)

Summary: Quick discovery to understand HelixAI's current OpenAI footprint, concerns around latency and cost, and appetite for Dedicated or Private deployment. They want to validate eval parity and run a perf POC (vLLM/TGI are in their stack).

[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone thanks for taking the time, quick intro, I'm Sofia from Redwood, Devon's our solutions engineer, we'll run through your current setup, goals, and what a migration might look like
[00:08] Marcus: Yeah thanks, I'm Marcus, CTO, Ravi will lead the ML questions, Ana our infra lead is here for the deploy stuff
[00:15] Ravi: Hey all, we currently use OpenAI for generation and Anthropic for some safety checks, roughly 1.2M tokens/day, spikes to 4M/day on product launches
[00:25] Devon: Got it. Do you use streaming and function calls with OpenAI or mostly standard completions?
[00:30] Ravi: A mix, streaming for chat UX, function-calls for structured outputs in a few microservices. We also do caching at the prefix level internally but it's not centralized
[00:40] Sofia: Great, high level: Redwood hosted gives you quick drop-in, Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools + SLA, Private gives a VPC/on-prem option with KMS for keys. Curious: what's driving this migration thought?
[00:52] Ana: Cost and predictability. OpenAI price increases make unit economics tricky at scale; and we want to reduce latency variance. Also security for some regulated customers, SSO and audit logs matter
[01:05] Ravi: Also eval parity. Our generation quality is tuned on specific OpenAI models and we need to ensure outputs match closely when we move to a different runtime or model family
[01:15] Devon: Totally. We do two things: 1) mapping compatibility layer for API semantics (so your function-calls and streaming map to Redwood endpoints) and 2) eval harnesses — we can run your prompt bank across candidate models and quantify regression metrics
[01:30] Marcus: You mentioned vLLM and TGI earlier — are those supported? We run a custom vLLM setup for internal dev and a TGI variant for lower-cost inference on some workloads
[01:40] Devon: Redwood's runtime is compatible with a lot of model variants; we often onboard models optimized by vLLM/TGI but note two things: kernel-level optimizations and quantization can change outputs slightly. Part of the POC is to run side-by-side A/B tests to measure delta
[01:55] Ravi: Ok that's fine, we need to define acceptable regression thresholds — like <2% BLEU change? we use a mix of BLEU-ish and human evals
[02:05] Sofia: We'll take your eval set and run our quality harness. We'll also include throughput and latency numbers per token. For Dedicated we can size based on your QPS and average seq length. What's your typical prompt length?
[02:18] Ravi: Average prompt+response ~450 tokens, but some flows hit 2k. P50 latency target from user request to first token is <250ms for chat flows
[02:28] Devon: For that target we'd look at model choice and batching policy. Dedicated helps reduce variance because you have isolated capacity, autoscaling and burst policies. For 250ms p50 at 450 tokens it's doable with an optimized model on A100 or H100 depending on throughput
[02:43] Ana: What about quantization and quality? We experimented with 8-bit and saw oddities in edge cases
[02:50] Devon: Yeah quantization can change outputs; we recommend running your evals across quantized profiles. Redwood Optimize will suggest quantization profiles tied to your workload and show predicted quality impact. We can also keep an unquantized fallback for critical routes
[03:05] Marcus: How intrusive is the migration? We have many microservices calling OpenAI endpoints directly — do we need to change code?
[03:12] Sofia: Most teams map to our API with minimal code change — we provide SDKs and a compatibility shim. For function-calls, streaming, embeddings it's usually a small wrapper. We'll share a migration guide and a compatibility checklist
[03:25] Ravi: And what about tokens and billing? We want transparent unit economics compared to OpenAI pricing
[03:30] Sofia: Dedicated pricing is typically reserved/committed capacity plus usage inside that pool. We can model cost per token given your volumes; that's part of the pricing doc I'll send. Also Redwood Console gives token-level breakdowns so you can see per-route cost
[03:44] Ana: Security — SOC2, SSO, KMS. Do you support customer-managed keys?
[03:49] Devon: Yes for Private we integrate with customer KMS/HSM; Dedicated can optionally use customer-managed keys for model artifacts and logs. We have SOC2 Type II and can share our compliance pack. There's also RBAC and audit logging in the console
[04:05] Ravi: Data residency — some customers require EU-only data. Do you support region pinning?
[04:10] Sofia: Yes region pinning and routing policies exist — you can route EU traffic to EU Dedicated/private pools. We'll document available regions and options
[04:18] Marcus: Perf POC — what's realistic? We want to test latency, throughput, and eval parity over a 2-week window
[04:25] Devon: Typical POC: 1) baseline collection (you send evals/traffic sample), 2) Redwood runs side-by-side inference on candidate model variants (hosted or dedicated nodes), 3) we run load profiles to simulate spikes, 4) we analyze regression and cost. Two weeks is doable if we scope it to key routes
[04:40] Ravi: For our stack we need support for streaming tokens and function calls with the same semantics as OpenAI — otherwise it complicates front-end logic
[04:49] Devon: We'll ensure streaming semantics match; minor differences can be shimmed client-side but we try to keep parity. We'll note any differences in the migration guide
[04:58] Ana: Who owns the rollout? Can we do canary and fallback to OpenAI if quality regresses?
[05:03] Sofia: Yes rollouts support canary, A/B and automated fallback. You can route a small percentage to Redwood and keep the bulk on OpenAI until satisfied. Console provides traces to compare responses
[05:15] Marcus: Any caveats migrating from Anthropic models? We use Anthropic for safety checks in a few flows
[05:21] Devon: That's a common pattern; we can keep Anthropic in the loop or run those safety checks on Redwood as well — depends on your compliance stance. We can test both in the POC
[05:32] Ravi: What about model licensing? If we want to run an Llama variant or community model, any restrictions?
[05:38] Devon: We respect model licenses; many open weights are supported but some commercial weights need agreements. We'll include model licensing notes in onboarding docs
[05:46] Ana: Operationally, what logs and metrics do we get? We need token-level billing, latency histograms, and trace links to requests
[05:53] Devon: Console includes per-route token breakdown, latency percentiles, error rates, and trace hooks you can integrate with your APM. Exporting logs to your SIEM is available for Private/Dedicated
[06:06] Marcus: Ok next steps?
[06:09] Sofia: We'll: 1) send pricing and capacity estimate, 2) security/compliance docs, 3) a migration checklist and compatibility shim, 4) schedule the technical deep dive and perf POC with Devon to scope model variants and metrics
[06:22] Ravi: Sounds good. We'll send eval prompts and a small traffic sample.
[06:26] Sofia: Perfect. Anything else?
[06:29] Ana: Can you include a note on HSM/KMS integration specifics — key rotation, supported providers?
[06:35] Devon: Yes I'll include supported KMS vendors and rotation patterns.
[06:38] Marcus: Great thanks everyone
[06:40] Sofia: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the docs and set up the technical session
